result.summary: In the Second Messenian War the armies clash and Aristomenes routs the Spartans, but loses his shield near a pear tree. He later recovers it at Trophonius's shrine, raids Pharae, and captures Spartan maidens at Caryae, protecting their honour.

scenes.title: Battle and the lost shield
scenes.summary: After sacrifices, the armies fight; Aristomenes and his picked men rout Anaxander's division, but he drops his shield at the pear tree and the Spartans recover, helped by Tyrtaeus.
scenes.stakes: Aristomenes risks losing the battle and his men's lives, and a fatal delay costs Messenian victory.

scenes.title: Return and recovered shield
scenes.summary: Aristomenes is welcomed at Andania with song, then recovers his shield through Delphi and Trophonius's shrine at Lebadea, where Pausanias saw it.

scenes.title: Raid on Pharae
scenes.summary: Aristomenes attacks Pharae by night, takes booty, and beats Anaxander's pursuing hoplites, though wounded by a javelin.
scenes.stakes: Aristomenes risks capture or death and loss of plunder when pursued by Spartans.

scenes.title: The maidens of Caryae
scenes.summary: Deterred from Sparta by divine apparitions, Aristomenes seizes maidens dancing at Caryae, kills unruly guards who try to violate them, and ransoms the girls unharmed.
scenes.stakes: The maidens' honour is in danger, and Aristomenes's discipline over his men.

alias_notes.explanation: Pharis is the Homeric name of the city the Spartans call Pharæ.

notable_quotes.reason: The women's victory song for Aristomenes, still sung in Pausanias's day.

analysis.text: Heroic valour is undone by neglected divine warning, yet the hero keeps his honour, shown by protecting the captive maidens.
Pausanias draws on Messenian tradition and his own visit to Lebadea, mixing local legend with personal observation.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias says he personally saw Aristomenes's shield, with its eagle, hanging at Lebadea.

language_notes.text: The sons of Aristodemus (Eurysthenes and Procles) were the Heraclid founders of Sparta's two royal houses; Hecas's ancestor came with them at the Dorian return.
The Iamidæ were a prophetic family of Elis claiming descent from Iamus, son of Apollo; Cresphontes, Messene's Heraclid king, brought them to Messene.
"In the very germ" means in their earliest stage, before the leader had fully formed or spoken them.
Castor and Pollux, the Dioscuri, were Spartan patron heroes, so the seer's warning implies Messenian defeat if he passes the tree.
Helots were the Spartans' serf class, descended from conquered Laconians and Messenians; here they are enrolled as soldiers.
Ribands are ribbons; the women decked Aristomenes with them as a mark of victory and honour.
Consulting the Pythian Priestess at Delphi was the usual way to learn a god's will; Trophonius's oracle at Lebadea involved descending into an underground chamber.
Homer's catalogue is the list of Greek forces in the Iliad, Book 2, which names Pharis among Menelaus's Laconian towns.
"Was fain to pursue" means he was eager or willing to pursue, an archaic use of "fain".
"Hinder quarters" is a delicate, old-fashioned way of saying his rear or buttocks.
Helen and the Dioscuri, Castor and Pollux, were Spartan divine figures; their apparition warned him off the city.

context_notes.text: Anaxander was a Spartan king during the Second Messenian War, with Aristomenes the great Messenian leader opposing him.
Tyrtæus was an Athenian-born poet whose war songs inspired Sparta; the Great Goddesses are Demeter and Persephone, whose priests accompanied the Messenian army.
Bœotia is the region of central Greece where Lebadea lay, far from Messenia.
Anaxander was a Spartan king during the Second Messenian War, as Pausanias tells it.
Caryae in Laconia had a sanctuary of Artemis where maidens performed ritual dances, making it a place where girls of good families gathered.

literary_notes.text: Fearless acceptance of wounds and reckless rushing heighten the heroic picture of Aristomenes' picked men.
Aristomenes' furious charges show him as a superhuman warrior, stronger than a single man should be.
Victory is undone by a small lapse: the hero's anger makes him ignore the prophecy and lose his shield.
Tyrtæus's revival of Spartan spirit anticipates the Messenians' eventual setback in the war.
Quoting a song still known in Pausanias's day links the legend to living tradition and lends it authority.
Pausanias adds his own eyewitness testimony, presenting himself as a traveller who verifies the legend with a surviving object.
Aristomenes' refusal to permit violation, and his killing of his own men, shows him as a man of honour and discipline.
